opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is just that the transformer is remarkably simple and remarkably general. When we wrote the original paper, we weren't trying to build something that would last a decade. We were trying to get rid of recurrence so we could parallelize training on the hardware we had. That turned out to be the key unlock: it maps beautifully onto GPUs and TPUs, and it scales really predictably. You add more data, more compute, more parameters, and it just keeps getting better.

Then there's the ecosystem effect, which people underestimate. At this point there's an enormous amount of infrastructure built around the transformer: kernels, inference stacks, training recipes, all the folk knowledge about initialization and learning rates and how to stabilize big runs. Any alternative architecture isn't just competing with the transformer as an idea. It's competing with years of collective engineering optimization. So it can't just be a little bit better on some benchmark. It has to be dramatically better to justify everyone tearing up their stack.

State-space models and the various linear-attention and recurrent variants are genuinely interesting, and they address a real weakness, which is the quadratic cost of attention over long contexts. But what we've seen is that the transformer tends to absorb the good ideas. You get hybrid architectures, you get better attention kernels, sparsity, sliding windows, and the efficiency gap narrows. Meanwhile, full attention has this property of being able to look back at anything in context with perfect fidelity, and for a lot of tasks like retrieval, reasoning, and copying, that really matters. Compressing everything into a fixed-size state is a real trade-off.

So I wouldn't say the transformer is the final architecture. I'd be surprised if it were. But displacing it requires something that changes the game at scale, not something that's marginally more efficient. And honestly, I think today the bigger gains are coming from data, from post-training, and from how we use these models, more than from swapping out the core block.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers absorb useful ideas from alternatives, including through hybrid architectures, which narrows the efficiency gap and reduces the case for replacing transformers with state-space models.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the staying power comes down to a couple of things, and only one of them is really about the architecture itself.

The first is that the transformer is just a very good fit for the hardware we have. It's almost embarrassingly parallel. Attention is a big matrix multiply, and GPUs and TPUs are matrix multiply machines. So every generation of accelerator that comes out makes transformers faster, and the people designing those chips are now explicitly optimizing for transformer workloads. It's a feedback loop. The architecture shaped the hardware and the hardware now entrenches the architecture.

The second is ecosystem lock-in, and I don't mean that as a criticism. Every optimization, every inference trick, every serving stack, every quantization method, all of it has been built around this one architecture. If you show up with a state-space model that's maybe ten or twenty percent better on some axis, you're competing against a decade of tooling that makes the transformer cheap and reliable to run. That's a really high bar to clear. You don't just need to be better, you need to be better by enough to justify rebuilding everything downstream.

And then the third thing, which I think people underweight, is that the transformer has turned out to be surprisingly malleable. When it had a weakness, like quadratic cost in context length, people didn't abandon it, they patched it. Flash attention, sparse attention, sliding windows, mixture of experts. The core idea keeps absorbing improvements without breaking.

Now, I actually think state-space models and the hybrid approaches are really interesting, and I wouldn't bet that what we're running in five years looks exactly like what we run today. The long-context and inference cost arguments for them are real. But what I expect is that transformers get hybridized rather than replaced. You take some attention layers, you take some recurrent or state-space layers, and you get the best of both. That's already happening. So in some sense the question of whether the transformer survives might be the wrong framing. It'll survive the way most good ideas do, by getting mixed into whatever comes next.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers will be hybridized rather than replaced, combining attention layers with recurrent or state-space layers to get the best of both.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how well transformers use the hardware we have. You can parallelize training very effectively, and we’ve built an enormous amount of infrastructure around making them fast. So an alternative has to compete with both the architecture and all the engineering behind it.

But attention also gives you a really useful capability: you can look back through the context and directly retrieve information that matters for the next prediction. With a state-space model, you’re generally compressing that history into a fixed-size state. That can be much more efficient, but it creates a tradeoff around what you retain and what you lose.

So I don’t think the staying power means transformers are the final answer. There are real costs, particularly with long contexts. I’d expect us to keep borrowing ideas from different architectures, potentially combining attention with other mechanisms. The question is whether you can get the efficiency gains while preserving the capabilities that make attention useful.

r001.rationale: The response suggests borrowing ideas from other architectures and combining mechanisms with attention, but it does not say this would eliminate the need to replace transformers with state-space models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how well transformers map onto the hardware we have. You can train them very efficiently, parallelize them, and keep scaling them. And there’s an enormous amount of accumulated knowledge about how to make them work well.

Attention also gives you a very useful capability: you can look back at a particular piece of context directly. If you’re compressing everything into a fixed-size state, you have to decide what to retain as you go. That can be a harder problem when some detail only becomes relevant much later.

That doesn’t mean state-space models won’t have a role. They have attractive efficiency properties, and hybrids could be really interesting. But an alternative has to beat a transformer that’s also continually improving. It’s not enough to have a nicer scaling curve on paper; you have to deliver a better model at a given cost.

r001.rationale: The response says hybrids could be interesting, but does not state that adding useful state-space model features to transformers would remove the need to replace transformers.
